articles.title: Here’s Why Everyone Is Talking About SNL’s “Sister” Skit—And Why Brothers Might Get a Talking-To at Thanksgiving This Year
articles.content: Holidays are the time for celebrating with family, catching up with loved ones and, if your family is anything like mine, discussing serious current events and buzzy pop-culture moments while we lie around in our PJs watching giant balloon animals. This Thanksgiving, those topics will no doubt include the election, the latest hit movies and one of our favorite shows, Saturday Night Live. My brother and I watched SNL religiously growing up, along with other late-night staples like Letterman and SCTV, so we’re always ready to argue over the relative merits of particular seasons. Well, these brother-sister dynamics might be put to the test this year, because SNL just dropped its most polarizing and hilarious sketch in years. If you haven’t heard about the latest skit, “Sister,” we have the entire thing below. Depending on your perspective, you may laugh nervously, nod vigorously or cry knowingly at the very real situation SNL pokes fun at. Read on for details on the outrageous sketch that’s taking over your social media feed right now and will likely come up at Thanksgiving dinner. Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more entertainment news, tech, humor, travel and fun facts all week long. The skit takes the form of a parody infomercial, with host John Mulaney addressing the camera like he’s about to sell you Medicare Part B. Over a backdrop of scenes of his elderly father, played by Tommy Brennan, Mulaney says he loves his dad and doesn’t want to see him go to a nursing home. And live-in care is expensive! “That’s when I heard about Sister,” he says to the camera. “Sister is a live-in, 24/7 elder-care provider that is completely free and also your sister.” To activate, all Mulaney has to do is text: “Dad fell.” Soon, cast member Jane Wickline shows up at their father’s house with a roller bag after quitting her job and breaking her lease. Other cast members, including Andrew Dismukes and Keenan Thompson, speak to the camera about how much they love their moms, but that doesn’t mean they want to help them in the bathroom or learn about their “confusing” medicines. Sister doesn’t either, “but she will, whereas I won’t,” Dismukes says. For brothers, it’s a win-win: “Now I don’t have to worry about my dad getting the care and attention he needs, because my sister will do it,” Mulaney says. “And I can get back to my life, and the stuff I like to do.” This skit hit a nerve, to say the least. Long-suffering, real-life “Sisters” took to social media to say they finally feel seen, while brothers and other siblings defended their own situations, which you know nothing about thank you very much! Sister partners, who also make an appearance in the skit, also related to this modern commentary on caregiving. “Speaking as someone who inadvertently found himself in the role of ‘Sister’s Husband,’ I can attest that this video is 100% accurate,” said someone on the official SNL YouTube channel. Very. Studies broadly support the idea that daughters are more likely than sons to take on caregiving roles for aging parents. According to a 2025 study by AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving, 61% of caregivers are women, compared to 38% of men. One particularly biting part of the skit touches on well-worn societal expectations of daughters. Mikey Day plays a doctor (and author of Not It! A Son’s Guide to Elder Care), who explains that “years of internalized sexism warp Sister’s brain into thinking caretaking is her responsibility, and somehow, not yours.” And in fact, studies bear this out. Multiple comprehensive reviews of the data, including one published in Research on Aging and another in the Journal of Family Theory & Review, found that parents more often expect daughters to provide eldercare. In one study, daughters were three times as likely as sons to have this expectation on them. Daughters also tend to model behavior from previous generations, which keeps the cycle going. Do something, brothers. Anything. (Like, please!) But seriously, just remember that the “Sister” skit rings true for a reason—your sister is probably facing more caregiving pressures than you. It’s not an indictment of all men, so avoid leaping to your gender’s defense while your older sister is organizing approximately 283 doctor’s appointments for your dad. And, in general, if you really want to avoid Sister’s wrath, skip saying things like “Mom doesn’t want me to see her like this.” News flash: She doesn’t want your sister to see her that way either. And younger sisters, you’re not off the hook either. Studies say that caregiving duties more often fall to the oldest sister, so if either of you have a big sis, check in with her. articles.summary:
Holidays are the time for celebrating with family, catching up with loved ones and, if your family is anything like mine, discussing serious current events and buzzy pop-culture moments while we lie around in our PJs watching giant balloon animals. This Thanksgiving, those topics will no doubt include the election, the latest hit movies and one of our favorite shows, Saturday Night Live.

My brother and I watched SNL religiously growing up, along with other late-night staples like Letterman and SCTV, so we’re always ready to argue over the relative merits of particular seasons. Well, these brother-sister dynamics might be put to the test this year, because SNL just dropped its most polarizing and hilarious sketch in years.

If you haven’t heard about the latest skit, “Sister,” we have the entire thing below. Depending on your perspective, you may laugh nervously, nod vigorously or cry knowingly at the very real situation SNL pokes fun at. Read on for details on the outrageous sketch that’s taking over your social media feed right now and will likely come up at Thanksgiving dinner.

Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more entertainment news, tech, humor, travel and fun facts all week long.

What is SNL’s “Sister” skit, exactly?

The skit takes the form of a parody infomercial, with host John Mulaney addressing the camera like he’s about to sell you Medicare Part B. Over a backdrop of scenes of his elderly father, played by Tommy Brennan, Mulaney says he loves his dad and doesn’t want to see him go to a nursing home. And live-in care is expensive!

“That’s when I heard about Sister,” he says to the camera. “Sister is a live-in, 24/7 elder-care provider that is completely free and also your sister.” To activate, all Mulaney has to do is text: “Dad fell.” Soon, cast member Jane Wickline shows up at their father’s house with a roller bag after quitting her job and breaking her lease.

Other cast members, including Andrew Dismukes and Keenan Thompson, speak to the camera about how much they love their moms, but that doesn’t mean they want to help them in the bathroom or learn about their “confusing” medicines. Sister doesn’t either, “but she will, whereas I won’t,” Dismukes says.

For brothers, it’s a win-win: “Now I don’t have to worry about my dad getting the care and attention he needs, because my sister will do it,” Mulaney says. “And I can get back to my life, and the stuff I like to do.”

What was the swift and brutally honest internet reaction?

This skit hit a nerve, to say the least. Long-suffering, real-life “Sisters” took to social media to say they finally feel seen, while brothers and other siblings defended their own situations, which you know nothing about thank you very much!

  • “As a caregiver, the SNL ‘Sister’ skit is actually a documentary,” said one put-upon caretaker on Threads.
  • “Omg, this is so true. I am the sister 😵‍💫,” said someone on Instagram.
  • “The best part are the two ‘Happy Birthday’ texts before ‘dad fell,’ showing how much he communicates with her,” said an observant YouTuber.
  • “Not even satire, a much needed public service announcement on how bad this sucks to be me. Thank you to the writers,” said another.

Sister partners, who also make an appearance in the skit, also related to this modern commentary on caregiving. “Speaking as someone who inadvertently found himself in the role of ‘Sister’s Husband,’ I can attest that this video is 100% accurate,” said someone on the official SNL YouTube channel.

How accurate is this family dynamic in real life?

Very. Studies broadly support the idea that daughters are more likely than sons to take on caregiving roles for aging parents. According to a 2025 study by AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving, 61% of caregivers are women, compared to 38% of men.

One particularly biting part of the skit touches on well-worn societal expectations of daughters. Mikey Day plays a doctor (and author of Not It! A Son’s Guide to Elder Care), who explains that “years of internalized sexism warp Sister’s brain into thinking caretaking is her responsibility, and somehow, not yours.” And in fact, studies bear this out.

Multiple comprehensive reviews of the data, including one published in Research on Aging and another in the Journal of Family Theory & Review, found that parents more often expect daughters to provide eldercare. In one study, daughters were three times as likely as sons to have this expectation on them. Daughters also tend to model behavior from previous generations, which keeps the cycle going.

If you’re a brother, what should you do now?

Do something, brothers. Anything. (Like, please!) But seriously, just remember that the “Sister” skit rings true for a reason—your sister is probably facing more caregiving pressures than you. It’s not an indictment of all men, so avoid leaping to your gender’s defense while your older sister is organizing approximately 283 doctor’s appointments for your dad.

And, in general, if you really want to avoid Sister’s wrath, skip saying things like “Mom doesn’t want me to see her like this.” News flash: She doesn’t want your sister to see her that way either. And younger sisters, you’re not off the hook either. Studies say that caregiving duties more often fall to the oldest sister, so if either of you have a big sis, check in with her.

Sources:

  • YouTube: “Sister—SNL”
  • @nbcsnl on Instagram
  • @noni.shiela on Threads
  • National Alliance for Caregiving: “Caregiving in the US Report 2025”
  • Research on Aging: “The Socialization of Unpaid Family Caregivers: A Scoping Review”
  • Journal of Family Theory & Review: “Expectations for Families to Care for Older Adults in the United States: Rapid Scoping Review 2011–2023”

articles.title: We Officially Have a New James Bond! Here’s Who Nabbed the 007 Role—And Which Huge Stars He Beat Out
articles.content:
As far as Hollywood casting announcements go, few get as much fanfare as 007 himself, James Bond. From the rugged Sean Connery to the comedic Roger Moore to the brooding Daniel Craig, the role has seen no fewer than six iterations since 1962, when Dr. No became the first movie based on Ian Fleming’s popular spy novels.
If you’re a 007 fan, you probably have a Bond you like best. I’m a Roger Moore gal, since he was the Bond of my childhood. My dad and I went to every Bond movie since For Your Eyes Only and caught the earlier ones whenever they were on TV. After quality turns by Timothy Dalton and Pierce Brosnan, the franchise went through a major overhaul in 2006 when Daniel Craig took the reins in Casino Royale.
But ever since Craig announced after No Time to Die, his fifth Bond film, that it was indeed time for his version of the character to die, Hollywood has been contemplating who would be the next British super spy. Well, we now have our answer. Read on to learn who will be the next Bond, James Bond, and which other big-name actors came really close to winning the part.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more movie news, tech, humor, travel and fun facts all week long.
Seemingly coming out of nowhere, James Pattinson will be the seventh actor to play the dashing British spy known as 007. Amazon MGM Studios made the announcement on Nov. 16, sending the entertainment press and Bond fans everywhere into a tizzy after years of speculation.
Pattinson, who is having a banner 2026 with four major releases, is, of course, a former teen idol known for playing vampire Edward Cullen in the Twilight franchise. But since the last Twilight installment in 2012, the actor has left teen roles behind him and become a respected performer in serious movies like The Lighthouse and Tenet, among many others (which we’ll get to in a minute).
So many actors! Earlier this year, the James Bond casting speculation centered around Jack Lowdon and Jack Barton, two up-and-comers who star in the buzzy British shows Slow Horses and Heartstoppers, respectively. Other contenders included Josh O’Connor, known to fans of The Crown and Challengers, and Callum Turner.
Lately, though, dark-horse speculation emerged around Nicholas Hoult, the former child actor (About a Boy) and X-Men actor who recently starred in The Great, and Pattinson. In early November, Variety reported that both actors screen-tested for the iconic 007 role, and now Pattinson has emerged victorious. Coincidentally, the two were also vying to play the newest Batman, and Pattinson got that job too.
Pattinson has been everywhere in 2026. You could barely go to the movies without seeing his face on the marquee, and he’s getting serious Oscar buzz for at least half of those projects (so far). That ratio is sure to increase with Dune: Part III, coming out before Christmas.
Here’s a peek at Robert Pattinson’s very good year:
And that’s just this year. In 2027, the new Bond will star alongside Denzel Washington and Daisy Edgar-Jones in a heist film called The Take, and filming is underway for 2028’s The Batman: Part II, with Pattinson reprising his role as Bruce Wayne (and Batman) in the sequel to the 2022 franchise reboot.
So far, Pattinson has kept his comments squarely in the PR realm. He called the role a “dream come true,” according to the Amazon press release. But in this case, it actually is! Way back in 2012, the actor, who was just coming off his run as the swoon-worthy Twilight vamp, gave an interview where he was specifically asked whether he would consider playing 007.
“Yeah, definitely,” he said to Shortlist. “But more like 20 years [from now]. There’d be nothing worse than, like, ‘Let’s get a fresh-faced Bond!’ That would be the worst idea in the world,” he continued, pointing to the big shoes he would be filling. “After Daniel Craig, you have to have some baggage. It would be ridiculous to reinvent it as some young posh kid. Or, if it was, I’d have to be tortured in the first few scenes. I’d have to do the first film with one arm or something.”
No word on the details, but since Pattinson has moved squarely from “young posh kid” to full-fledged adult actor, we don’t think that one-armed guess is likely. As any Bond fan knows, though, first-scene introductions are critical to getting the audience on board. Craig famously emerged from the surf in a nod to another former Bond icon, Ursula Andress, and we hope that Pattinson can pull off a similar feat.

articles.title: 16 Practical Emergency Preparedness Supplies for Peace of Mind
articles.content:
When severe weather hits your area, having a reliable source of information can be just as important as having food and water. A NOAA weather radio lets you receive official weather alerts and emergency updates even when your internet connection is down or cellular networks are overwhelmed.
Look for a radio with automatic weather alerts, backup battery power and Specific Area Message Encoding (SAME), which lets you receive warnings for your local area. Hand-crank or solar charging capabilities give you an additional way to power the device when electricity is out.
“One of the most overlooked emergency preparedness items is a reliable way to receive information when normal communications are disrupted,” says Joshua Shanley, an emergency management professor at Purdue Global and retired firefighter-paramedic with more than 35 years of experience in emergency services.
Flashlights are essential during a blackout, but a headlamp is arguably even more practical. By keeping both hands free, it makes everything from navigating dark stairways to tending to children and gathering supplies considerably easier. I keep a two-pack of these BIAT headlamps ready to go in my house and end up using them quite often (letting the dog out at night—great for two-handed poop scooping!).
Greg Pearson, founder and CEO of Focus Point International, an emergency response and evacuation services company, recommends choosing a headlamp that’s simple to operate, even while wearing gloves.
“For a flashlight or headlamp, battery life and a simple switch matter more to me than extreme brightness,” Pearson explains. Look for adjustable brightness, water resistance and a comfortable head strap. Ideally, every household member should have their own light source.
A dead phone battery is the last thing you want during an emergency. A portable power bank gives you a way to recharge your phone, tablet or other small electronics when outlets aren’t available.
For most households, Shanley suggests starting with a power bank that pumps out 10,000 to 20,000 milliamp-hours (mAh) of capacity. Larger models can provide additional charges, while built-in cables and multiple USB ports make it easier to power several devices. The Anker model I recommend here has an impressive 25,000 mAh in a nifty compact package.
Solar charging can be useful, too, but it shouldn’t be your only way to recharge. Keep your power bank charged, store the necessary cables alongside it and test it with your devices every now and then so you know it still works.
Storing drinking water is an important part of emergency preparedness, but having a way to treat additional water gives you another layer of protection if your regular supply runs out.
Portable water filters range from compact squeeze-style devices to larger gravity-fed systems that can serve multiple people without electricity. However, not all filters provide the same protection, and it’s important to understand their limitations before relying on one.
“For a water filter, read what it actually removes,” advises Pearson. “A filter that improves taste may offer no protection against germs, and many portable filters don’t remove viruses.”
Look for independently tested filtration systems with certifications appropriate for the contaminants you’re concerned about. Remember that portable filters generally cannot make water contaminated with fuel or other hazardous chemicals safe to drink. Always follow local drinking-water advisories.
A first aid kit is useful even when there isn’t an emergency, but it’s especially valuable when storms, flooding or power outages make medical care harder to access.
A good household kit should contain supplies for common injuries, including adhesive bandages, sterile gauze, dressings, antiseptic wipes, medical gloves and basic wound-care tools. You may also want to add personal medications and other supplies specific to your family’s needs.
Shanley recommends prioritizing practical supplies that everyone in the household knows how to use. There’s not much benefit to buying a fancy med kit packed with equipment you don’t know how to use. Check expiration dates regularly and replace anything you’ve used so it’s ready the next time you need it.
While a flashlight is useful for getting around, a lantern can light up a larger area, making it easier to cook, eat, play games or spend an evening together when the lights go out.
Battery-powered LED lanterns are more practical for indoor emergencies than candles, which come with an unnecessary fire risk. Look for a model with adjustable brightness, long battery life and a stable base or hanging hook. Rechargeable lanterns are convenient, but models that also accept replaceable batteries give you another option during extended outages.
A lantern is particularly helpful for families, providing a shared light source that doesn’t need to be carried from room to room.
Carbon monoxide is an odorless, colorless gas that can be deadly, and the risk of exposure increases when people start using fuel-powered generators or alternative heating methods during a blackout.
A working carbon monoxide detector is an important safety device for any home. Choose one with battery backup or independent battery power so it can keep working when electricity is unavailable. Make sure it meets applicable safety standards and follow the manufacturer’s instructions for installation and replacement.
Pearson emphasizes that a detector is an additional safeguard, not a substitute for safe generator operation. Fuel-powered generators should always be operated outdoors, at least 20 feet from doors, windows and vents, with exhaust directed away from the home.
Important documents probably aren’t the first things that come to mind when preparing for a storm, but losing them can make an already difficult situation even more complicated.
A waterproof document bag or pouch can help protect copies of identification, insurance policies, medical information, property records and emergency contact lists. Some models can also be fire-resistant, although protection levels vary, so it’s worth verifying the manufacturer’s claims and testing information.
Guerrero recommends keeping copies of essential paperwork in an accessible location while storing originals securely. Digital backups are also smart, but a physical copy is unbeatable when your phone is dead or the internet is down.
You never know what small problem might crop up during an emergency. A compact multi-tool keeps several of them in one place, potentially saving you from rummaging through a toolbox in the dark.
Look for a sturdy model with practical features such as pliers, screwdrivers, a knife and a can opener. These can help with minor repairs, opening packages, cutting materials and other everyday tasks when normal routines are disrupted.
Keep it somewhere accessible and familiarize yourself with it before an emergency. There’s no need to invest in an oversized survival tool with dozens of attachments you’ll never use. A reliable, straightforward design is usually the better choice.
It’s not the most glamorous emergency supply, but sanitation becomes a major concern when running water, sewer service or normal waste collection is interrupted.
Basic supplies such as heavy-duty trash bags, disposable gloves, hand sanitizer, wet wipes and toilet paper can make a big difference. For longer disruptions, a portable toilet or emergency waste bags can be helpful, particularly if you area is prone to flooding.
Guerrero recommends including sanitation supplies in every household emergency kit, noting that these everyday necessities can become difficult to access when services are disrupted. Choose compact items that are easy to store, and make sure you have a plan for handling waste safely if your plumbing becomes unusable.
This inexpensive little device is easy to overlook, but it can save you from guessing whether the contents of your fridge are still safe after a prolonged power outage.
According to the FDA, an unopened refrigerator typically keeps food cold for about four hours without electricity, while a full freezer can maintain its temperature for approximately 48 hours. Keeping an appliance thermometer inside each compartment helps you monitor temperatures and keep on top of food safety.
Pearson recommends putting thermometers in place before an outage so the information is available when you need it. Look for easy-to-read models designed specifically for refrigerators and freezers, and follow official food-safety guidance when deciding what to keep or throw out.
A sturdy pair of work gloves might not seem like emergency equipment, but they can come in handy when clearing small branches, moving debris or handling rough materials after a storm.
Choose gloves that offer a good balance of protection and dexterity. Reinforced palms, abrasion-resistant materials and a secure fit are useful features, particularly if you’ll be working outdoors. Depending on the task, additional protection such as safety glasses and sturdy, closed-toe footwear may also be necessary.
Gloves don’t make dangerous cleanup work safe, however. Avoid downed power lines, unstable structures, floodwater and other hazardous debris, and leave major storm damage to trained professionals.
Don’t forget about your vehicle. If you need to evacuate or travel during a widespread power outage, a dead car battery could leave you stranded at exactly the wrong time.
A portable jump starter lets you restart your vehicle without needing another car and a set of jumper cables. Many models also include USB charging ports and built-in flashlights, making them useful additions to a vehicle emergency kit.
Choose one with enough starting power for your engine, straightforward safety features and a battery-level indicator. Store it according to the manufacturer’s temperature recommendations and check its charge regularly (especially before storm season).
Summer blackout and no air conditioning? No thanks! A battery-operated fan won’t replace your AC, but it can give you some welcome airflow when the house starts getting stuffy. I own this BougeRV model and it has never failed me. I also love the soft glowing light on it, so it’s multifunctional (and the battery lasts over 30 hours!).
Compact rechargeable fans are easy to move between rooms, while larger models offer better circulation. Look for adjustable speeds, a stable base and enough battery life to run for several hours. Some models also double as power banks or include built-in lighting.
Keep in mind that fans alone aren’t enough protection from extreme heat. If indoor temperatures become unsafe, particularly for older adults, young children or people with health conditions, seek an air-conditioned location.
For those looking to invest in more substantial emergency backup power, a portable power station can be a worthwhile upgrade from a standard phone charger. I’ve tested several brands, and I think Bluetti’s new Apex 200 strikes a great balance between portability and power when needed.
Irrespective of brand, these large rechargeable batteries can run or recharge devices ranging from phones and laptops to fans, lights and certain small appliances. Higher-capacity models may also support refrigerators or other essential equipment for a limited time, depending on their power requirements.
Pay attention to both battery capacity, measured in watt-hours (Wh), and output capacity, measured in watts (W). Battery capacity helps determine how long a device can run, while output determines what equipment the power station can handle. Some models can also recharge from compatible solar panels.
Unlike fuel-burning generators, battery power stations don’t pump out toxic gas when you’re using them, so they’re great for indoor backup power when used according to the manufacturer’s instructions. However, they don’t last forever, and anyone relying on electrically powered medical equipment should have a backup plan specifically designed for that device.
Portable Generator
A portable generator is one of the bigger investments on this list, but it can be extremely valuable if you experience frequent or prolonged power outages.
Depending on the model’s capacity, a generator can keep essential appliances running, power a refrigerator or provide electricity to selected household circuits. Conventional portable generators typically run on gasoline, while dual-fuel models can operate on gasoline or propane. I recently reviewed Anker’s tri-fuel generator and would easily recommend it as one of the best portable generators available.
Before buying, consider how much power you’ll actually need, fuel storage, noise levels, maintenance requirements and safe installation. Look for models with carbon monoxide shutoff technology, and never operate a fuel-powered generator indoors, in a garage or near windows and doors. A qualified electrician should install appropriate transfer equipment if you plan to connect one to household wiring.
Shanley cautions against investing in expensive emergency equipment simply because it seems impressive. Instead, he recommends focusing on realistic household needs and choosing reliable equipment you know how to operate.
Putting together an emergency kit is a great start, but that doesn’t do much good if the batteries are dead, supplies have expired or nobody remembers where everything is stored.
Guerrero recommends inspecting your supplies at least twice a year, testing equipment, recharging power banks and replacing expired items. Keep everything in a dry, accessible location that every household member knows about, and consider packing a smaller bag with essentials in case you need to evacuate quickly.
As Pearson puts it, “If I weren’t home, would everyone else know where this stuff is and how to use it?” That’s a much better measure of preparedness than how much equipment you own.

NOAA Weather Radio

Midland WR400 Deluxe

Shop on Amazon

Shop on Walmart

Shop on Target

When severe weather hits your area, having a reliable source of information can be just as important as having food and water. A NOAA weather radio lets you receive official weather alerts and emergency updates even when your internet connection is down or cellular networks are overwhelmed.

Look for a radio with automatic weather alerts, backup battery power and Specific Area Message Encoding (SAME), which lets you receive warnings for your local area. Hand-crank or solar charging capabilities give you an additional way to power the device when electricity is out.

“One of the most overlooked emergency preparedness items is a reliable way to receive information when normal communications are disrupted,” says Joshua Shanley, an emergency management professor at Purdue Global and retired firefighter-paramedic with more than 35 years of experience in emergency services.

LED Headlamp

BIAT Rechargeable LED Headlamp

Shop on Amazon

Shop on Walmart

Flashlights are essential during a blackout, but a headlamp is arguably even more practical. By keeping both hands free, it makes everything from navigating dark stairways to tending to children and gathering supplies considerably easier. I keep a two-pack of these BIAT headlamps ready to go in my house and end up using them quite often (letting the dog out at night—great for two-handed poop scooping!).

Greg Pearson, founder and CEO of Focus Point International, an emergency response and evacuation services company, recommends choosing a headlamp that’s simple to operate, even while wearing gloves.

“For a flashlight or headlamp, battery life and a simple switch matter more to me than extreme brightness,” Pearson explains. Look for adjustable brightness, water resistance and a comfortable head strap. Ideally, every household member should have their own light source.

Portable Power Bank

Anker Laptop Power Bank

Shop on Amazon

Shop on Anker

A dead phone battery is the last thing you want during an emergency. A portable power bank gives you a way to recharge your phone, tablet or other small electronics when outlets aren’t available.

For most households, Shanley suggests starting with a power bank that pumps out 10,000 to 20,000 milliamp-hours (mAh) of capacity. Larger models can provide additional charges, while built-in cables and multiple USB ports make it easier to power several devices. The Anker model I recommend here has an impressive 25,000 mAh in a nifty compact package.

Solar charging can be useful, too, but it shouldn’t be your only way to recharge. Keep your power bank charged, store the necessary cables alongside it and test it with your devices every now and then so you know it still works.

Water Filtration System

LifeStraw Gravity Filter System

Shop on Amazon

Shop on LifeStraw

Storing drinking water is an important part of emergency preparedness, but having a way to treat additional water gives you another layer of protection if your regular supply runs out.

Portable water filters range from compact squeeze-style devices to larger gravity-fed systems that can serve multiple people without electricity. However, not all filters provide the same protection, and it’s important to understand their limitations before relying on one.

“For a water filter, read what it actually removes,” advises Pearson. “A filter that improves taste may offer no protection against germs, and many portable filters don’t remove viruses.”

Look for independently tested filtration systems with certifications appropriate for the contaminants you’re concerned about. Remember that portable filters generally cannot make water contaminated with fuel or other hazardous chemicals safe to drink. Always follow local drinking-water advisories.

First Aid Kit

100-Person First Aid Kit

Shop on Amazon

A first aid kit is useful even when there isn’t an emergency, but it’s especially valuable when storms, flooding or power outages make medical care harder to access.

A good household kit should contain supplies for common injuries, including adhesive bandages, sterile gauze, dressings, antiseptic wipes, medical gloves and basic wound-care tools. You may also want to add personal medications and other supplies specific to your family’s needs.

Shanley recommends prioritizing practical supplies that everyone in the household knows how to use. There’s not much benefit to buying a fancy med kit packed with equipment you don’t know how to use. Check expiration dates regularly and replace anything you’ve used so it’s ready the next time you need it.

Battery-Powered Lantern

Coleman 800-Lumen LED Lantern

Shop on Amazon

Shop on Coleman

Shop on Walmart

While a flashlight is useful for getting around, a lantern can light up a larger area, making it easier to cook, eat, play games or spend an evening together when the lights go out.

Battery-powered LED lanterns are more practical for indoor emergencies than candles, which come with an unnecessary fire risk. Look for a model with adjustable brightness, long battery life and a stable base or hanging hook. Rechargeable lanterns are convenient, but models that also accept replaceable batteries give you another option during extended outages.

A lantern is particularly helpful for families, providing a shared light source that doesn’t need to be carried from room to room.

Carbon Monoxide Detector

Carbon Monoxide Detector With Battery Backup

Shop on Amazon

Shop on Home Depot

Shop on Walmart

Carbon monoxide is an odorless, colorless gas that can be deadly, and the risk of exposure increases when people start using fuel-powered generators or alternative heating methods during a blackout.

A working carbon monoxide detector is an important safety device for any home. Choose one with battery backup or independent battery power so it can keep working when electricity is unavailable. Make sure it meets applicable safety standards and follow the manufacturer’s instructions for installation and replacement.

Pearson emphasizes that a detector is an additional safeguard, not a substitute for safe generator operation. Fuel-powered generators should always be operated outdoors, at least 20 feet from doors, windows and vents, with exhaust directed away from the home.

Waterproof Document Bag

SentrySafe Fire and Water Resistant Bag

Shop on Amazon

Shop on Lowe's

Shop on Walmart

Shop on Ace Hardware

Important documents probably aren’t the first things that come to mind when preparing for a storm, but losing them can make an already difficult situation even more complicated.

A waterproof document bag or pouch can help protect copies of identification, insurance policies, medical information, property records and emergency contact lists. Some models can also be fire-resistant, although protection levels vary, so it’s worth verifying the manufacturer’s claims and testing information.

Guerrero recommends keeping copies of essential paperwork in an accessible location while storing originals securely. Digital backups are also smart, but a physical copy is unbeatable when your phone is dead or the internet is down.

Multi-Tool

Leatherman Wave Plus Multi-Tool

Shop on Leatherman

Shop on Amazon

You never know what small problem might crop up during an emergency. A compact multi-tool keeps several of them in one place, potentially saving you from rummaging through a toolbox in the dark.

Look for a sturdy model with practical features such as pliers, screwdrivers, a knife and a can opener. These can help with minor repairs, opening packages, cutting materials and other everyday tasks when normal routines are disrupted.

Keep it somewhere accessible and familiarize yourself with it before an emergency. There’s no need to invest in an oversized survival tool with dozens of attachments you’ll never use. A reliable, straightforward design is usually the better choice.

Emergency Sanitation Kit

Ann Katy Portable Toilet 30-Pack

Shop on Amazon

It’s not the most glamorous emergency supply, but sanitation becomes a major concern when running water, sewer service or normal waste collection is interrupted.

Basic supplies such as heavy-duty trash bags, disposable gloves, hand sanitizer, wet wipes and toilet paper can make a big difference. For longer disruptions, a portable toilet or emergency waste bags can be helpful, particularly if you area is prone to flooding.

Guerrero recommends including sanitation supplies in every household emergency kit, noting that these everyday necessities can become difficult to access when services are disrupted. Choose compact items that are easy to store, and make sure you have a plan for handling waste safely if your plumbing becomes unusable.

Refrigerator and Freezer Thermometer

Taylor Analog Thermometer

Shop on Amazon

Shop on Ace Hardware

This inexpensive little device is easy to overlook, but it can save you from guessing whether the contents of your fridge are still safe after a prolonged power outage.

According to the FDA, an unopened refrigerator typically keeps food cold for about four hours without electricity, while a full freezer can maintain its temperature for approximately 48 hours. Keeping an appliance thermometer inside each compartment helps you monitor temperatures and keep on top of food safety.

Pearson recommends putting thermometers in place before an outage so the information is available when you need it. Look for easy-to-read models designed specifically for refrigerators and freezers, and follow official food-safety guidance when deciding what to keep or throw out.

Heavy-Duty Work Gloves

Ironclad Utility Work Gloves

Shop on Amazon

A sturdy pair of work gloves might not seem like emergency equipment, but they can come in handy when clearing small branches, moving debris or handling rough materials after a storm.

Choose gloves that offer a good balance of protection and dexterity. Reinforced palms, abrasion-resistant materials and a secure fit are useful features, particularly if you’ll be working outdoors. Depending on the task, additional protection such as safety glasses and sturdy, closed-toe footwear may also be necessary.

Gloves don’t make dangerous cleanup work safe, however. Avoid downed power lines, unstable structures, floodwater and other hazardous debris, and leave major storm damage to trained professionals.

Portable Jump Starter

NOCO Boost BG40

Shop on Amazon

Shop on Walmart

Don’t forget about your vehicle. If you need to evacuate or travel during a widespread power outage, a dead car battery could leave you stranded at exactly the wrong time.

A portable jump starter lets you restart your vehicle without needing another car and a set of jumper cables. Many models also include USB charging ports and built-in flashlights, making them useful additions to a vehicle emergency kit.

Choose one with enough starting power for your engine, straightforward safety features and a battery-level indicator. Store it according to the manufacturer’s temperature recommendations and check its charge regularly (especially before storm season).

Battery-Operated Fan

BougeRV Portable Rechargeable Fan

Shop on Amazon

Shop on BougeRV

Summer blackout and no air conditioning? No thanks! A battery-operated fan won’t replace your AC, but it can give you some welcome airflow when the house starts getting stuffy. I own this BougeRV model and it has never failed me. I also love the soft glowing light on it, so it’s multifunctional (and the battery lasts over 30 hours!).

Compact rechargeable fans are easy to move between rooms, while larger models offer better circulation. Look for adjustable speeds, a stable base and enough battery life to run for several hours. Some models also double as power banks or include built-in lighting.

Keep in mind that fans alone aren’t enough protection from extreme heat. If indoor temperatures become unsafe, particularly for older adults, young children or people with health conditions, seek an air-conditioned location.

Portable Power Station

Bluetti Apex 200

Shop on Bluetti

For those looking to invest in more substantial emergency backup power, a portable power station can be a worthwhile upgrade from a standard phone charger. I’ve tested several brands, and I think Bluetti’s new Apex 200 strikes a great balance between portability and power when needed.

Irrespective of brand, these large rechargeable batteries can run or recharge devices ranging from phones and laptops to fans, lights and certain small appliances. Higher-capacity models may also support refrigerators or other essential equipment for a limited time, depending on their power requirements.

Pay attention to both battery capacity, measured in watt-hours (Wh), and output capacity, measured in watts (W). Battery capacity helps determine how long a device can run, while output determines what equipment the power station can handle. Some models can also recharge from compatible solar panels.

Unlike fuel-burning generators, battery power stations don’t pump out toxic gas when you’re using them, so they’re great for indoor backup power when used according to the manufacturer’s instructions. However, they don’t last forever, and anyone relying on electrically powered medical equipment should have a backup plan specifically designed for that device.

Portable Generator

Portable Generator

Anker Tri-Fuel Smart Generator 5500

Shop on Anker

Shop on Amazon

A portable generator is one of the bigger investments on this list, but it can be extremely valuable if you experience frequent or prolonged power outages.

Depending on the model’s capacity, a generator can keep essential appliances running, power a refrigerator or provide electricity to selected household circuits. Conventional portable generators typically run on gasoline, while dual-fuel models can operate on gasoline or propane. I recently reviewed Anker’s tri-fuel generator and would easily recommend it as one of the best portable generators available.

Before buying, consider how much power you’ll actually need, fuel storage, noise levels, maintenance requirements and safe installation. Look for models with carbon monoxide shutoff technology, and never operate a fuel-powered generator indoors, in a garage or near windows and doors. A qualified electrician should install appropriate transfer equipment if you plan to connect one to household wiring.

Shanley cautions against investing in expensive emergency equipment simply because it seems impressive. Instead, he recommends focusing on realistic household needs and choosing reliable equipment you know how to operate.

How to Keep Your Emergency Supplies Ready

Putting together an emergency kit is a great start, but that doesn’t do much good if the batteries are dead, supplies have expired or nobody remembers where everything is stored.

Guerrero recommends inspecting your supplies at least twice a year, testing equipment, recharging power banks and replacing expired items. Keep everything in a dry, accessible location that every household member knows about, and consider packing a smaller bag with essentials in case you need to evacuate quickly.

As Pearson puts it, “If I weren’t home, would everyone else know where this stuff is and how to use it?” That’s a much better measure of preparedness than how much equipment you own.

About the Experts

  • Joshua Shanley is an emergency management professor at Purdue Global and retired firefighter-paramedic with more than 35 years of experience in emergency services.
  • Greg Pearson is the founder and CEO of Focus Point International, an emergency response and evacuation services company.
  • Rangel Guerrero is the public safety director for St. Lucie County, Florida and has more than 20 years of public safety and emergency management experience.

Sources

  • FDA: Safe Food Handling

articles.title: This Is the Most Popular Thanksgiving Dessert in Each State—Did Your Favorite Nab the Top Spot?
articles.content:
In my family, Thanksgiving rules. For the past 30-plus years, my brother, sister, mom and I pick a place we can all get to from our far-flung locations, and we meet up to cook a traditional Thanksgiving spread. Well, I cook, and the rest of the clan lounges around drinking coffee and watching the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade.
I’ve made a Thanksgiving turkey in a tiny Philadelphia galley kitchen, a green bean casserole at a log cabin in the Ozarks and mashed potatoes and gravy at several random Las Vegas timeshares and Airbnbs (we took a cab to the grocery store one year). But no matter how terrible the kitchen utensils are, I always make a pumpkin pie, an apple pie and, lately, a pecan pie too.
This Thanksgiving trifecta of dessert pies covers everyone’s bases—especially mine, since I hate pumpkin pie and practically get the apple pie all to myself. What about you? Do you cook (or buy, no shame) a traditional after-turkey-dinner treat, or does your family like something a little more off the beaten path? DoorDash decided to answer this question for families across the nation, and coming up, we have the surprising answers.
Read on to discover which Thanksgiving desserts are tops nationally, as well as state by state, and get ready to dig in.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more food, holidays, humor, travel and fun facts all week long.
DoorDash looked at orders between Nov. 19 and Nov. 27, 2025, to see just what sweets Americans were hungry for on Thanksgiving. Compiling data from retail, restaurant and grocery-store DoorDash orders, they compared national trends with state data to determine how traditional Thanksgiving desserts like pumpkin, pecan and apple pies fared next to up-and-comers like cake.
The results are literally all over the map here, with pumpkin pie rubbing shoulders with other dessert giants more commonly seen at your kid’s birthday party. Here’s how the data shook out.
Traditional Thanksgiving-dessert lovers can rest easy, because pumpkin pie came out on top in 14 states, or more than a quarter (28%) of the country. Other fall-flavored pies scored as well, with pecan pie winning four states and apple pie three. But as you’ll see below, some interesting nontraditional dessert trends appear to be gaining steam.
If you’ve ever woken from your post-turkey nap craving chocolate instead of pumpkin pie, you have plenty of company. In the national rankings, chocolate cake was the most-ordered dessert during DoorDash’s Thanksgiving buying period, knocking pumpkin pie all the way down to fourth. Apple pie ranked second, while cheesecake (?) sat comfortably in third.
Could Thanksgiving become a major chocolate-themed holiday? All signs point to yes. In addition to the overwhelming national win, chocolate cake won five individual states. Meanwhile, chocolate pie was tops in six states and made the national list at No. 6 overall.
Move over, Rust Belt, because you will henceforth be called the Cheesecake Belt. Eight states, from West Virginia and Ohio all the way over to the Midwestern states of Minnesota and Iowa, sat down to cheesecake for Thanksgiving last year. Wisconsin was the lone pumpkin-pie holdout in the entire region, which is a little surprising given its fame as America’s Dairyland.
The West also showed up big for pumpkin pie. Aside from Wisconsin, every state that went for pumpkin pie—13 out of 14—is west of the Mississippi River. Pecan pie stuck to its Southern roots, winning in Texas, Oklahoma, Louisiana and Tennessee, while apple pie’s three wins came (appropriately) in New York as well as Massachusetts and Connecticut.
Let’s talk about pound cake. This old-fashioned, dense buttery cake turned up as the top dessert choice for Thanksgiving in an astounding six states, more popular than both apple and pecan pie. It also made the top five nationally. If it seems like a strange choice for not only Thanksgiving but just in general, half a dozen states and your grandmother would like a word.
We already talked about chocolate cake, but its birthday-and-wedding partner in crime, vanilla cake, also did surprisingly well in DoorDash’s annual Thanksgiving report. It won three states in the coastal Atlantic region: Virginia, North Carolina and South Carolina.
Finally, Georgia went way out on a limb this year, and that limb belongs to a Key lime tree. The tart, custardy Key lime pie was the No. 1 most popular Thanksgiving dessert in the Peach State—a place where Key limes only grow with some help because they do not fare well in Georgia winters.

What’s the most popular Thanksgiving dessert in each state?

The results are literally all over the map here, with pumpkin pie rubbing shoulders with other dessert giants more commonly seen at your kid’s birthday party. Here’s how the data shook out.

  • Texas: Pecan pie
  • Utah: Cheesecake
  • Vermont: Chocolate pie
  • Virginia: Vanilla cake
  • Washington: Pumpkin pie
  • West Virginia: Cheesecake
  • Wisconsin: Pumpkin pie
  • Wyoming: Chocolate cake

Which Thanksgiving dessert earned the No. 1 spot in the most states?

Traditional Thanksgiving-dessert lovers can rest easy, because pumpkin pie came out on top in 14 states, or more than a quarter (28%) of the country. Other fall-flavored pies scored as well, with pecan pie winning four states and apple pie three. But as you’ll see below, some interesting nontraditional dessert trends appear to be gaining steam.

Apple pie ranked second, while cheesecake (?) sat comfortably in third.

Could Thanksgiving become a major chocolate-themed holiday? All signs point to yes. In addition to the overwhelming national win, chocolate cake won five individual states. Meanwhile, chocolate pie was tops in six states and made the national list at No. 6 overall.

What regional trends emerged?

Move over, Rust Belt, because you will henceforth be called the Cheesecake Belt. Eight states, from West Virginia and Ohio all the way over to the Midwestern states of Minnesota and Iowa, sat down to cheesecake for Thanksgiving last year. Wisconsin was the lone pumpkin-pie holdout in the entire region, which is a little surprising given its fame as America’s Dairyland.

The West also showed up big for pumpkin pie. Aside from Wisconsin, every state that went for pumpkin pie—13 out of 14—is west of the Mississippi River. Pecan pie stuck to its Southern roots, winning in Texas, Oklahoma, Louisiana and Tennessee, while apple pie’s three wins came (appropriately) in New York as well as Massachusetts and Connecticut.

Were there any other big surprises?

Let’s talk about pound cake. This old-fashioned, dense buttery cake turned up as the top dessert choice for Thanksgiving in an astounding six states, more popular than both apple and pecan pie. It also made the top five nationally. If it seems like a strange choice for not only Thanksgiving but just in general, half a dozen states and your grandmother would like a word.

We already talked about chocolate cake, but its birthday-and-wedding partner in crime, vanilla cake, also did surprisingly well in DoorDash’s annual Thanksgiving report. It won three states in the coastal Atlantic region: Virginia, North Carolina and South Carolina.

Finally, Georgia went way out on a limb this year, and that limb belongs to a Key lime tree. The tart, custardy Key lime pie was the No. 1 most popular Thanksgiving dessert in the Peach State—a place where Key limes only grow with some help because they do not fare well in Georgia winters.

articles.title: Watch The Reader’s Digest Escalator Interview with Actor and Author Tony Shalhoub
articles.content: Whether you know him as the lovable, obsessive-compulsive detective Adrian Monk from Monk, the hilariously opinionated Abe Weissman from The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel or from big-screen favorites like Big Night, Men in Black and Galaxy Quest, chances are Tony Shalhoub has made you laugh at least once (and probably a whole lot more). With a career spanning more than four decades, the beloved actor has earned four Emmy Awards, a Golden Globe and a Tony Award for his Broadway performance in The Band’s Visit. Now, he’s adding another title to his impressive résumé: author. And this time, the stories he’s telling hit a little closer to home. For this episode of The Reader’s Digest Escalator Interview, we caught up with Shalhoub to talk about his new book, We Thought They’d Never Leave: Musings on Food and Family, co-written with his daughter, Josie Adams. Part love letter to family culinary traditions (with 20 original recipes included for good measure) and part personal narrative, the book takes readers inside the Shalhoub family’s famously large gatherings in Wisconsin. “A lot of it is about the family reunion that we have every year, that we’ve had for the last 50-odd years,” Shalhoub tells us. “The numbers have grown to ridiculous size.” But family stories are just the appetizer. Shalhoub also reveals what he’s currently reading, some of his favorite authors and one hilariously specific thing he’s particular about in real life. And that’s not all he had to share.
